curriculum.title: HTTP, REST & JSON
curriculum.outcome: Trace requests from client to server
curriculum.lesson:
An HTTP request has a method, URL, headers and sometimes a body. GET reads a representation; POST commonly creates a resource. JSON is a data format, not a transport. A useful task API returns 201 with a resource identifier on creation, 200 on retrieval and a clear 400 response for malformed input. Record the request and response together.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: trace requests from client to server.
Implement the Day 1 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.
curriculum.assignment: Build a small task API with GET and POST; save one successful and one invalid request.

questions.prompt: Which status best describes a newly created task?
questions.explanation: 201 Created.

questions.prompt: Your POST creates a task. What should the response include?
options: 404 because the task did not exist before
A redirect to an unrelated page
questions.explanation: 201 and the new task identifier.

curriculum.title: Authentication & API contracts
curriculum.lesson:
Authentication establishes who is calling; authorization decides what that caller may do. A valid login does not grant access to every record. Validate the request schema and check ownership on the server for every operation. An OpenAPI document describes methods, inputs, outputs and error responses; it does not enforce permissions by itself.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: separate authentication from authorization.
Implement the Day 2 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.
curriculum.assignment: Add token authentication, request validation and an OpenAPI contract; show a rejected unauthorized request.

questions.prompt: What should happen when a valid user requests another user’s private record?
options: The API trusts the submitted user ID
The server rejects it after checking ownership
The client hides the link only
questions.explanation: The server rejects it after checking ownership.

questions.prompt: A valid token belongs to learner A, who requests learner B’s private submission. What next?
options: Trust an ownerId supplied in the request
Reject access after an ownership check
Return it because the token is valid
Ask the browser to hide it after loading
questions.explanation: Reject access after an ownership check.

curriculum.title: Transformers, tokens & context
curriculum.outcome: Explain context limits and token costs
curriculum.lesson:
A transformer processes token representations using attention. Tokens are model-specific units rather than words or characters. The context window limits what information a request can use; including a fact in yesterday’s conversation does not mean a new request contains it. Measure tokens with the selected model’s tokenizer and record the model and input alongside the measurement.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: explain context limits and token costs.
Implement the Day 3 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.
curriculum.assignment: Compare token counts for three prompts and document what happens when relevant context is removed.

questions.prompt: What consumes a model’s context budget?
options: Input and generated output within the model’s limits
Only characters in the user’s name
questions.explanation: Input and generated output within the model’s limits.

questions.prompt: Two models tokenize the same text differently. How do you compare usage?
options: Record counts with each model’s tokenizer and identifier
Assume every word equals one token
Use one model’s count for both without qualification
questions.explanation: Record counts with each model’s tokenizer and identifier.

curriculum.title: Prompt design & baselines
curriculum.lesson:
A useful prompt states the task, relevant context, constraints and output contract. Establish a baseline before adding examples or extra instructions. Compare versions on fixed inputs using a predefined criterion. Keep development examples separate from your final evaluation set so you do not mistake tuning to known examples for general improvement.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: make instructions testable.
Implement the Day 4 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.
curriculum.assignment: Write a prompt with a clear task, constraints and output format; compare it on five fixed examples.

questions.prompt: How should two prompt versions be compared?
options: With the same held-out examples and scoring rules
questions.explanation: With the same held-out examples and scoring rules.

questions.prompt: Prompt B looks better on one hand-picked example. What can you conclude?
options: B eliminates the need for validation
Only B’s longer output proves improvement
More fixed evaluation cases are needed
questions.explanation: More fixed evaluation cases are needed.

curriculum.title: LLM API & structured outputs
curriculum.lesson:
Put model requests behind a small adapter so application logic can be tested without a live paid model. Structured output is still untrusted input: validate types, required fields, ranges and business rules. A response that parses as JSON may still be invalid for your application. Define a controlled error for malformed or incomplete results.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: validate model responses before use.
Implement the Day 5 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.

questions.prompt: What protects downstream code from malformed model data?
options: Parsing text by its font size
Schema validation plus explicit failure handling
questions.explanation: Schema validation plus explicit failure handling.

questions.prompt: A response is valid JSON but its score is outside the permitted range. What next?
options: Accept it because JSON parsing succeeded
questions.explanation: Reject it using business-rule validation.

curriculum.title: Retries, latency & budget
curriculum.lesson:
Transient failures need bounded recovery. Use a timeout, a limited retry count and backoff for retryable errors. Track total elapsed time as well as individual attempts. Retrying a write can duplicate side effects, so combine retries with idempotency where appropriate. Record usage and pricing assumptions instead of treating an estimated cost as a billed amount.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: bound failure recovery and spending.
Implement the Day 6 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.

questions.prompt: Which retry strategy is safest?
options: Bounded retries with backoff and a total timeout
questions.explanation: Bounded retries with backoff and a total timeout.

questions.prompt: A request keeps receiving rate limits. Which behavior is appropriate?
options: Hide the failures and report success
Back off and stop at the retry or time budget
questions.explanation: Back off and stop at the retry or time budget.

curriculum.title: What makes an agent?
curriculum.outcome: Distinguish a fixed workflow from a decision loop
curriculum.lesson:
A fixed workflow follows branches chosen by application code. An agent loop allows a model to select a next action from an allowed set. Use an agent when that flexibility serves the task; deterministic code is often easier to test for a fixed procedure. Both approaches need explicit inputs, outputs, permissions and stopping conditions.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: distinguish a fixed workflow from a decision loop.
Implement the Day 7 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.
curriculum.assignment: Compare a scripted workflow and an agent loop on the same task; explain when each is appropriate.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an agent loop?
options: Model decisions can select the next allowed action
questions.explanation: Model decisions can select the next allowed action.

questions.prompt: A task always follows the same three known steps. What is a useful baseline?
options: A deterministic workflow implementing those steps
A model with unrestricted filesystem access
A system with no acceptance criteria
questions.explanation: A deterministic workflow implementing those steps.

curriculum.title: Tool schemas & validation
curriculum.lesson:
A tool is a capability with a contract. Narrow tools such as get_task(id) are easier to validate than arbitrary commands. Define required properties, types, bounds and whether extra arguments are rejected. Validation belongs at the execution boundary even when the model was given a schema. Return actionable errors without exposing credentials.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.

Implement the Day 8 practical exercise and record its output.

questions.prompt: Where should tool arguments be validated?
options: Never if the model is capable
questions.explanation: At the server-side tool boundary.

questions.prompt: A tool expects an integer ID but receives a shell command string. What next?
options: Execute it to infer the intended ID
Pass it through because the schema was in the prompt
questions.explanation: Reject it before tool execution.

curriculum.title: Function calling
curriculum.lesson:
Function calling asks the model for a tool name and arguments; your application decides whether to execute them. Dispatch through an explicit allowlist, validate arguments and preserve call identifiers when returning results. A model-generated name is not permission to run shell code. Test both an unknown name and invalid arguments.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: dispatch only allowed tools.
Implement the Day 9 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.

questions.prompt: How should an unknown tool call be handled?
options: Reject it with a controlled error
questions.explanation: Reject it with a controlled error.

questions.prompt: The model requests delete_everything, which is absent from your tool registry. What next?
options: Run the name as a command
questions.explanation: Return an unknown-tool error.

curriculum.title: ReAct & observable steps
curriculum.outcome: Inspect actions without requiring hidden reasoning
curriculum.lesson:
ReAct connects observations and actions in a repeated task process. For debugging, log observable tool names, validated arguments, durations, results and concise decision summaries. Hidden chain of thought is unnecessary. A trace should let you locate the failed boundary and reproduce the problem while redacting secrets and sensitive payloads.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: inspect actions without requiring hidden reasoning.
Implement the Day 10 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.

questions.prompt: Which log is useful for debugging an agent?
options: A demand for hidden chain of thought
Observable tool calls, results and errors
questions.explanation: Observable tool calls, results and errors.

questions.prompt: Which trace helps reproduce a failed lookup?
options: A screenshot of a success icon
Call ID, validated input, status, duration and redacted error
questions.explanation: Call ID, validated input, status, duration and redacted error.

curriculum.title: Agent loop & stop conditions
curriculum.lesson:
Every loop needs code-enforced limits: maximum steps, wall-clock deadline and an explicit final-result contract. Stop when the goal is achieved, the budget is exhausted or a required capability is unavailable. A prompt saying do not loop forever is not a runtime guard. Test a mock that repeatedly requests the same tool.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: keep execution bounded.
Implement the Day 11 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.

questions.prompt: What prevents an endless tool loop?
options: A step cap and deadline enforced by code
questions.explanation: A step cap and deadline enforced by code.

questions.prompt: The model has used every allowed step without a final answer. What next?
questions.explanation: Stop with a budget-exhausted result.

curriculum.title: Failures & recovery
curriculum.lesson:
Classify failures before recovering. Invalid input usually needs correction; a temporary network error may justify a bounded retry; missing permission requires rejection or user action. Preserve the failed operation and its error in the trace. Verify whether a write already happened before repeating it. A partial result should identify what remains incomplete.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: make tool errors actionable.
Implement the Day 12 practical exercise and record its output.
Test a failure case and document what you learned.

options: When it can repeat a side effect without idempotency
When the error message is short
When the tool has a name
questions.explanation: When it can repeat a side effect without idempotency.

questions.prompt: A timed-out write might already have succeeded. What must recovery consider?
options: Only whether the error message is short
Retrying with a new identifier each time
Operation status and an idempotency key
questions.explanation: Operation status and an idempotency key.

curriculum.title: Single-agent checkpoint
curriculum.lesson:
A checkpoint is evidence that a bounded system meets stated criteria. For your research helper, define five cases with expected behavior, including unavailable tools or unsupported claims. Use mock responses to make tests repeatable, then label any optional live-model runs separately. Record failures as well as successes in the demonstration.

options: Repeatable cases with stated success criteria and failures
questions.explanation: Repeatable cases with stated success criteria and failures.

questions.prompt: One of five fixed research-helper cases fails. How should it be reported?
options: Remove the failed case without explaining why
Replace the result with a hypothetical answer
Four successes and the observed failure with its cause
questions.explanation: Four successes and the observed failure with its cause.

curriculum.title: Embeddings & similarity
curriculum.lesson:
Embeddings map inputs into vectors whose distances can approximate semantic relatedness. Similarity depends on the embedding model and does not prove truth, recency or access permission. Compare relevant and irrelevant queries against known documents. Record the model, similarity measure and retrieved identifiers so the experiment can be reproduced.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.
objectives: Explain: explain what semantic distance represents.
Implement the Day 14 practical exercise and record its output.

questions.prompt: What does embedding similarity indicate?
options: Proof that a claim is current
Approximate semantic relatedness under the chosen model
questions.explanation: Approximate semantic relatedness under the chosen model.

questions.prompt: A retrieved document has high embedding similarity. What remains unproven?
options: That a similarity score was computed
Its factual correctness and access authorization
questions.explanation: Its factual correctness and access authorization.

curriculum.title: Chunking & retrieval
curriculum.lesson:
Chunking determines what units retrieval can return. Small chunks may lose context; large chunks may mix relevant and irrelevant passages. Hold queries and the embedding model fixed while changing chunk size. For a small labelled set, measure whether the known relevant passage appears among the top k results before adding a generator.

questions.explanation: Check whether known relevant passages are retrieved.

options: The effect of chunk size is confounded by model changes
The experiment automatically becomes more accurate
Recall no longer needs relevant labels
The larger chunk must be better
questions.explanation: The effect of chunk size is confounded by model changes.

curriculum.title: Grounded answers & citations
curriculum.outcome: Keep answers tied to retrieved evidence
curriculum.lesson:
Retrieval augmented generation supplies retrieved evidence to a model. Keep the document identifier, excerpt and any useful timestamp with each passage. Ask for claims supported by that evidence and verify citations against the actual text. If retrieval misses the answer, generating a confident sentence does not repair the evidence gap.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.

options: Flag the unsupported claim and revise or qualify it
questions.explanation: Flag the unsupported claim and revise or qualify it.

curriculum.title: Memory lifecycle & RAG review
curriculum.lesson:
Memory has scope and a lifetime. Session context, durable preferences and retrieved documents serve different purposes. Store only what is useful, preserve its origin and permit correction or removal. A timestamp helps identify stale evidence. Never retrieve another person’s private memory merely because it is semantically similar to the current query.

curriculum.title: Agents SDK setup
curriculum.lesson:
An SDK packages model calls, tool dispatch and run state, but the application still owns its business rules. Start with one minimal agent and capture its final result. Keep tools and validation testable independently of a model provider. Pin and document the SDK version before following examples because interfaces can change.

curriculum.title: SDK tools & validation
curriculum.lesson:
SDK tools should expose the same clear contracts as standalone functions. Use descriptive names, typed inputs and structured failures. Test the underlying function directly, then test registration and dispatch separately. A tool description helps selection; it does not replace validation or authorization. Keep side effects explicit in both documentation and tests.

curriculum.title: SDK handoffs & boundaries
curriculum.lesson:
A handoff transfers responsibility to a specialist with a narrower purpose. Define the trigger, the input summary and the tools the specialist may use. A vague handoff can lose constraints or expand permissions accidentally. Include a test where the coordinator should keep the task instead of transferring every request.

Work through the linked primary documentation, then implement today's exercise. Use mocks or a local model when needed. Keep a working example, a failed case and a short explanation of what the results demonstrate.

questions.explanation: Keep it with the appropriate agent or ask for clarification.

curriculum.title: Traces & observability
curriculum.lesson:
Observability connects events across a run using stable identifiers. Capture status, tool latency, failures and selected non-sensitive metadata. Logging everything can expose private inputs or keys. Seed a fake secret in a test and verify redaction. Distinguish a trace of what happened from a claim that the result was correct.

curriculum.title: LangGraph state & nodes
curriculum.outcome: Model a workflow as typed state
curriculum.lesson:
A state graph models nodes as operations over explicit shared state. Document which fields each node consumes and produces. Treat a state transition as a contract that can be tested with a fixed input. Avoid hidden globals that disappear on restart or cause one run to affect another.

questions.prompt: A node reads a field never defined in graph state. What should be fixed?

curriculum.title: Conditional routing
curriculum.lesson:
Conditional routing chooses an edge from the current state. Give each branch a clear predicate and define a fallback for uncertain or invalid cases. Test retrieval, tool and clarification paths independently. When a model proposes the route, validate its output against allowed labels before following an edge.

curriculum.title: Checkpoints & human review
curriculum.lesson:
A checkpoint stores enough workflow state to resume from a known point. Place a human review boundary before a consequential write. On resumption, check that the reviewed inputs have not changed and that repeating the operation will not duplicate it. Process memory alone is not a durable checkpoint.

curriculum.title: Framework comparison
curriculum.lesson:
Compare frameworks using the same task and acceptance criteria. Examine how each handles state, tool failures, tests, resumption and deployment. Count code and setup effort only as secondary signals. The useful conclusion explains which tradeoffs fit this task; it should not claim one framework is universally best.

curriculum.title: Multi-agent task decomposition
curriculum.lesson:
Decomposition helps when specialists have independent responsibilities and explicit outputs. Split a research task into evidence retrieval, claim checking and synthesis only if the boundaries reduce complexity. Specify a shared result schema and a budget. A specialist dependent on another result cannot safely start with an invented input.

Whenever more tokens can be spent

curriculum.title: Coordinator & specialists
curriculum.lesson:
A coordinator assigns bounded work, checks output contracts and decides when the task is done. Specialists should have only the capabilities needed for their roles. Enforce maximum delegation depth, task count and time budget in code. Test a specialist failure so the coordinator can return an honest partial result.

curriculum.title: Shared state & messages
curriculum.lesson:
Concurrent agents can overwrite the same record. Use stable identifiers and a version or transaction check to detect conflicts. Define a typed message containing sender, task, status and result. When two updates conflict, preserve the conflict and reconcile it explicitly instead of silently treating the last message as correct.

curriculum.title: Parallel work & aggregation
curriculum.lesson:
Parallel execution reduces waiting only when tasks are independent. Aggregate successes and failures in a structured result, preserving which specialist produced each part. A failed task should remain visible. Compare latency and output quality with a sequential baseline; adding more agents can increase cost without improving the answer.

curriculum.title: Disagreement & verification
curriculum.lesson:
Specialists can disagree because they used different evidence, definitions or assumptions. Resolve factual claims by checking original sources and the scope of each claim. Majority voting is not verification. Preserve uncertainty when the sources do not resolve it and cite the evidence used in the final response.

curriculum.title: MCP concepts
curriculum.outcome: Separate host, client and server roles
curriculum.lesson:
MCP separates a host application, a client connection and a server exposing capabilities. Tools perform operations; resources expose contextual content; prompts provide reusable interaction templates. An MCP connection does not automatically reveal all chat history. Keep your progress service independent of transport so its rules remain directly testable.

curriculum.lesson:
A tool schema describes accepted arguments and helps a client present the operation. Pair it with server-side validation and an explicit result shape. curriculum.lesson:

curriculum.lesson:
An HTTP-hosted tool server may handle each request on a different instance. Durable state belongs in a database rather than a module variable. curriculum.title: OAuth & authorization
curriculum.outcome: Bind access to the correct resource
curriculum.lesson:
OAuth delegates access to a defined resource with limited permissions. PKCE binds authorization-code redemption to the initiating client. Validate token issuer, audience, expiry and permissions at the trusted boundary or use a platform that enforces them. Keep tokens outside URLs and client bundles. A successful login alone is not record authorization.

curriculum.lesson:
Read and write are different capabilities. A progress reader should not submit work or approve assignments. Enforce the distinction on the server, not only in tool descriptions. Test that a read-only caller is rejected when it attempts a write. Final approval can be a separate learner-controlled action even when a reviewer suggests scores.

Store the workspace identifier independently of the caller identity and retain the actor for auditing. Verify both invited identities see the same record while an uninvited caller is rejected by the access boundary.

curriculum.lesson:
Integration tests should exercise the actual boundaries between identity, protocol handling, validation and persistence. curriculum.lesson:
An evaluation dataset contains representative inputs and predefined expected behavior. Include routine tasks, ambiguous requests and failure cases. Record provenance and exclusions. curriculum.lesson:

curriculum.lesson:

curriculum.lesson:
An idempotency key identifies one logical write across retries. Repeating the same key and payload should return the previous result; reusing a key for a different operation should conflict. Persist the key with the operation and enforce uniqueness atomically. Checking first without handling a simultaneous insertion leaves a race.

curriculum.lesson:
Security tests should match the product’s actual data and capabilities. Try unauthorized reads, invalid writes and malicious retrieved instructions. Assert what must remain unchanged after rejection. A cosmetic UI check cannot establish authorization. Document the boundary tested and the limits of local mocks.

curriculum.title: Performance & cost budget
curriculum.lesson:
Measure latency and cost on representative cases before optimizing. Record p50 and p95 only when the sample size supports useful interpretation, and disclose small samples. Separate model time, retrieval and tool execution. Set explicit budgets and test behavior when a request reaches them.

curriculum.title: Deploy & recover
curriculum.lesson:
A release needs a known revision, migration plan and recovery procedure. Export records, restore them into a separate test environment and compare key fields. A file named backup is not proof of recoverability. Keep production credentials separate and document any manual steps honestly.

curriculum.title: User acceptance & iteration
curriculum.lesson:
User acceptance checks whether the main workflow serves its intended user. Observe a walkthrough, record reproducible failures and map them to acceptance criteria. Fix the issue that blocks the primary task before adding decoration. Re-run the failed criterion after the change and retain the result.

curriculum.title: Documentation & portfolio evidence
curriculum.lesson:
Documentation should let another developer run the project and understand its limits. Include setup, architecture, environment variable names, evaluation results and a short demo script. Keep keys and private learning records out of the repository. Distinguish implemented behavior from planned features.
